subject: physics
title: Photons and the electronvolt
key_idea: Electromagnetic radiation travels as waves but is emitted and absorbed in packets of energy called photons. A photon's energy is E = hf, so it rises with frequency. The electronvolt is the energy unit that suits photons and electrons.

blocks.text: Electromagnetic radiation has a wave model and a photon model. Each explains different observations.

items: The **wave model** explains interference and diffraction, which only waves show.
The **photon model** explains how radiation is emitted and absorbed: in particles, one at a time.
Both models are needed. Neither is complete alone.

items.meaning: A packet, or quantum, of electromagnetic energy.
The smallest amount of energy that can be exchanged. Plural: quanta.

blocks.text: The models developed over time. Light was first pictured as particles, then shown to behave as waves. Einstein later used photons to explain the photoelectric effect.

items: A photon carries one fixed quantum of energy.
A photon is not a tiny ball with mass: it has no rest mass and always travels at the speed of light.
A beam is a stream of photons. A brighter beam has more photons each second, not bigger ones.
Electromagnetic radiation is emitted and absorbed as photons.
A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic energy.
Wave behaviour and particle behaviour are two models of the same radiation.

blocks.text: The energy of one photon depends only on the frequency of the radiation. Higher frequency means more energy.
The wave equation c = fλ links frequency and wavelength. Substituting it gives the energy in terms of wavelength.

items: A blue photon has more energy than a red photon, because blue light has a higher frequency.
A gamma ray photon has far more energy than a radio photon.
Long wavelength means low photon energy.

diagram.alt: A slider showing that photon energy rises as wavelength falls. Move the wavelength and read the frequency and photon energy.

items: E = hf: photon energy is proportional to frequency.
E = hc/λ: photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

blocks.text: Photon and electron energies are tiny in joules. The electronvolt is a more convenient unit.

items.meaning: The energy gained by one electron when it is accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt.

blocks.label: Converting eV to joules
where: 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the charge of one electron, e

items.text: Multiply the energy in eV by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹.
Divide the energy in joules by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹.

items: A visible photon has an energy of about 2 to 3 eV.
Use the eV for atomic and photon energies, and joules when you substitute into equations such as E = hf.

diagram.question: A photon has a frequency of {f} × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate its energy in eV. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

items: Convert eV to J before using E = hf with h in J s.

checks.q: Calculate the energy in joules of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
State what is meant by a photon.
Explain why an ultraviolet photon has more energy than an infrared photon.
checks.a: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency (shorter wavelength). Since E = hf, a higher frequency means a larger photon energy.

blocks.text: A photon also has momentum, even though it has no mass. Its momentum is its energy divided by the speed of light.

blocks.label: Photon momentum
where: p = momentum of the photon (kg m/s)

items: Since E = hf = hc/λ, this gives p = h/λ.
Shorter wavelength means more momentum.
The momentum of one photon is very small, about 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s for visible light.
A photon has momentum p = E/c.
For a photon, p = h/λ.

extra.heading: Estimating the Planck constant with LEDs

blocks.text: A light-emitting diode starts to conduct when each electron gains enough energy to make one photon. This gives a way to estimate h.

items: Increase the potential difference across the LED slowly until it just begins to glow.
Record this threshold potential difference V.
Measure the wavelength λ of the light from the LED with a diffraction grating, or use its stated value.
Repeat with LEDs of different colours.
Plot V against 1/λ for the different LEDs. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
The gradient is hc/e, so h = gradient × e / c.
No knowledge of semiconductor theory is needed.
eV = hc/λ for an LED at the threshold.
Plot V against 1/λ and use the gradient to find h.
